label: text
text: HOUR TO HOUR POINTS

label: text
text:
Yesterday was the third day of the general strike.
London's crowds were in a gay mood. Vehicles were more numerous, but traffic jams were fewer.

label: text
text: Emergency services are rapidly improving. There is a great increase in passenger trains. The London tubes are reopening.

label: text
text: There is no shortage of food and little attempt made to raise prices.

label: text
text: Little difficulty is experienced in securing drivers for transport. London taximen decided to join the strike.

label: text
text: A serious conflict between the crowd and the Police occurred in Edinburgh.

label: text
text: Overseas cable communications will not be impeded by the strike.

label: text
text: Buses: were attacked in South London, volunteer drivers and conductors being roughly handled.

label: text
text: Seven big London newspapers and 30 provincial papers published emergency editions, whilst 22 provincial evening papers published the usual editions

label: text
text: strong intimidation in the Eastern district of London has prevented some movement of foodstuffs. The Trades Union Congress denies this and states that its orders as regards milk and foodstuffs have generally been loyally obeyed.

label: text
text: orries, leaving Southampton for London are being turned back by pickets.

label: text
text: (imprisonment of a week to three months has been imposed on hooligans at Old Street Police Court.

label: text
text: The P. & O. and the B.I. shipping companies are tackling the problem of conveying overseas passengers from Tilbury and Albert Docks to their home destinations.

label: text
text: In a communique the Government says that abundant food and ample transport are available.

label: text
text: warning is issued that all at-tempts by pickets to impede the free movement of the people or their food will be methodically and firmly repressed.

label: text
text: Local authorities are asked to follow the Government's policy of refusing co-operation from the general strike organisers.

label: text
text: the debate on the Emergency Regulations, Labour amendments being rejected by overwhelming majorities.

label: text
text: Mr. Batey saw in the regulation dealing with protection of property an attempt to enable the mine owners to fill the pits with blacklegs.

label: paragraph_title
text: PRICE, $3.00 Per Month.

label: text
text: Sir Douglas Hogg said that the suggestion that the people should not be allowed to carry on their business because a body of Trade Unionists had forbidden it was the best justification for this regulation. Mr. Mardy-Jones hotly declared that the Miners' Federation took up Sir Douglas Hogg's challenge.

label: text
text: In the debate on another regulation Mr. Thurtle indulged in dark threats: For every turn of the thumb-screw the Government gave to-day Labour would give back ten!

label: text
text: Eventually the Labourites left the House.

label: text
text: Insurance against damage by rioters and strikers remaining steady at rates showing no panic tendency.

label: text
text: Disorderly scenes occurred in the Old Kent Road District, a private car being set on fire.

label: text
text: Mr. S. Saklatvala, the Communist M.P., was sentenced to two months for a seditious speech, refusing to find sureties.

label: text
text: “We are with you in your fight, cables General Lee Bullar from New York to Mr. Baldwin”

label: text
text: BLUE SKIES.

label: text
text: (Reuter's Service.)

label: text
text: Blue Summer skies on the third morning of the strike found vast crowds going to business in London in a gaymood. "Vehicles were more numerous than ever. But traffic jams were fewer, partly due to the drivers following the back streets hitherto unexplored.

label: text
text: The principal centres of interest in the newspaper world are the offices of the "Daily Mail" and "Daily Herald" outside which crowds still gather, whilst outside the "Morning Post" office, where the "British Gazette" is published, a number of evident strikers congregate. There is no disorder, but the gates are shut by the Police on duty.

label: paragraph_title
text: EMERGENCY SERVICES

label: text
text: The emergency services are rapidly improving in all directions. A great increase is reported in passenger trains on the main local lines and trunk lines which are now running 300 to 400 trains daily.

label: text
text: The London tubes are reopening to-day.

label: text
text: Government reports state that, speaking generally, there is no shortage of food. Apparently there has been little effort to raise prices. There is no difficulty in obtaining drivers for transport as anticipated by the Civil Commissioner. In some cases where there is difficulty in moving supplies the Trades Union Congress has permitted volunteer workers to remove the goods.

label: paragraph_title
text: Tüximen to Strike.

label: text
text: The London taximen decided to join the strike at midnight yesterday but hundreds were on the streets this morning.

label: text
text: A conflict occurred late last night in Edinburgh between a big crowd and the Police when bottles and stones were thrown. Shop windows were smashed and the contents of two looted.

label: text
text:
Five constables and a number of
ivilians were sent to hospital. A
olice Sergeant was slashed on the
ack with a razor.

label: text
text: A mounted constable's horse took fright and bolted. It collided with a railing and was killed. The rider was severely injured.

label: text
text: It can authoritatively be stated that there is no likelihood of the strike impeding overseas cable communications.

label: text
text:
A mob attacked some buses near the Elephant and Castle, South London. They set fire to one manned by a volunteer driver and conductor, who were forced to dismount, being roughly handled as they endeavoured to get clear. The passengers were told to disembark beforehand. The Police galloped to the scene, and constables and special constables soon controlled the situation.
The driver and conductor of another bus who were waylaid and nearly crashed into the Elephant public house, were also forced to fly to safety.

label: paragraph_title
text: Buies Attacked.

label: paragraph_title
text: ACCIDENTS:

label: text
text:
Emergency papers.
In addition to the London newspapers already mentioned emergency editions were issued to-day of the "Daily Telegraph," Daily Mail, "Daily Express," Daily Mirror, "Financial News," Financial Times and "Evening News." London Hospital

label: text
text: A motor cycle driven by Marine Barnicott with Marine Freeman on the pillow seat met with an accident at Bus Vaux Road West this morning.

label: text
text: In passing a hand truck Freeman knocked his leg on one of the wheels, injuring it below the knee. He was taken direct on board H.M.S. "Taman."

label: paragraph_title
text: Lorry Collision

label: text
text: Two lorries collided in the New Territories yesterday and one of them ran into a paddy field. The driver of the vehicle escaped serious injury.

label: text
text: In his report, the driver states that he was proceeding between Taipo and Fanling, when another lorry owned by the Luon Hop Transportation Company struck his vehicle in passing and overturned it into the paddy field. He scrambled out to find that the other lorry had disappeared. Damage to the extent of $40 was done to the vehicle.

label: paragraph_title
text: Drowned.

label: text
text: A Chinese boy, seven years old, living with his father at No. 110, Portland Street, Yaumati, lost his life yesterday afternoon by falling into a pool of water on the reclamation at Argyle Street.

label: text
text: Some people in the vicinity pulled the boy out and artificial respiration was tried by a Chinese doctor without effect. The Kwong Wah Hospital authorities declared life to be extinct when the body was taken there shortly after.

label: paragraph_title
text: Another Fatality.

label: text
text: A coolie living at the Ho Leong contractors' matshed at Robinson Road, died in hospital yesterday. The man is believed to have died from the effects of poisoning, as it was found on inquiry that he had taken some boiled herbs which he obtained from a medicine dealer at Tung Street.

label: paragraph_title
text: London Hospital has been closed owing to strike difficulties.

label: text
text: According to a Government statement there has been strong intimidation in the Eastern district preventing some movement of foodstuffs.

label: text
text: Between 70 and 80 London omnibuses did not return to the depots on scheduled time last night owing to damage to various parts, but 50 more General omnibuses are operating to-day.

label: text
text: "Lorries going to London from Southampton are being turned back by pickets."

label: text
text: Trade Union Denial

label: text
text: The Council of the Trades Union Congress report to-day that the solidarity of the workers has been maintained all over the country, but denies that food supplies have been up. On the other hand the Council's orders as regards milk and foodstuffs have generally been loyally obeyed.

label: text
text: Imprisonment ranging from a week to six months has been imposed at Old Street Police Court arising out of strike scenes at Shoreditch and Bethnal Green, including assaults on the Police.

label: text
text: More Newspapers Appearing. Twenty-two provincial evening papers published the usual editions and 80 published emergency editions. Eight exhibited news notices. In Glasgow the papers issued joint editions.

label: text
text: Edinburgh Disturbances. Three of the men arrested during last night's disturbances in Edinburgh were sent to prison for a month or fined.

label: text
text: Overneas Passengers.

label: text
text:
Enquiries made of the F. & P. and British-India Steamship Companies show that they are fully alive to the problem of conveying passengers arriving at Tilbury and Albert Docks from overseas to Home destinations.
The Companies consider that it is not desirable to publish the nature of these arrangements, particularly in view of the fact that the area is in the heart of dock land and an amount of intimidation is possible, but they give an assurance that everything possible is being

label: paragraph_title
text: FINAL WITNESSES.

label: text
text: SPEECHES TO FOLLOW.

label: text
text: Final witnesses for the second prisoner were called this morning in the Wing On Bank case and the case was adjourned until Monday morning for the speeches and summing up to follow without a week-end break.

label: text
text: Witnesses were called in support of the second prisoner's statement that Tam Lay, the man who spoke with regard to certain chops, the Crown allege, were forged for the purpose of the alleged conspiracy, was never employed at the engraving and printing shop kept by the second prisoner. They all denied having seen Tam Lay before.

label: text
text:
Witnesses were all cross-examined by Mr. Jenkin as to the kind of types used by the shop.
Chan Kau, a young apprentice who had at times entered in the books of the printing shop in Canton, was handed sheets of paper with pieces cut out through which a certain amount of writing underneath could be discerned. He was asked by Mr. Jenkin if he could identify the writing.
In each case witness said he could not until the paper was removed. The writing was then seen to be in certain account books of the firm whereupon witness stated that it was either in the writing of the second prisoner himself or of another employee. Chan Chau. The writing of the two was very similar.

label: text
text: Mr. Jenkin: So similar that it is practically impossible to distinguish the two?

label: text
text: Witness: I cannot tell the difference.

label: text
text: Mr. Jenkin: I put it to you that the whole of the writing is in the hand of Chan Chau, the man who fetched these books from Canton. Witness: That is not so.

label: text
text:
Mr. Ho Chuk-pang, whose name had been mentioned by the principal witness for the prosecution (Chan Sam) as a man whom the second prisoner had visited in the company of himself (Chan Sam) for the purpose of raising money in connection with the civil action which was to be brought against the Wing On Bank, was produced on subpoena for the defence.
He stated that he did not know the second prisoner and had never received a visit from him in company with Chan Sam for the purpose of raising money. Chan Sam had called in connection with raising money but the second prisoner was not with him.

label: text
text: Witness was cross-examined by Mr. Jenkin as to his relations with a man named Ah Hong. He admitted he knew a man of that name but denied that he had ever given him money.

label: text
text: Witness was asked by Mr. Jenkin to write the name Ah Hong on a piece of paper.

label: text
text: This being done, witness was handed an envelope by Mr. Jenkin in which there was a slit with writing showing. Witness was asked if it was his own writing, Witness replied that it was.

label: text
text: The writing underneath was, been shown in full and purported to be a letter to a Mr. Li Yukum to give Ah Hong the sum of 30.

label: text
text:
was for Ah Hong to bring to him (witness) and not for Ah Hong himself.
“Suggestions.”
At the close of the cross-examination of witnesses, Mr. Jenkin referred to what he termed suggestions that had been made in the course of the hearing with regard to the label on “Nina,” it having been stated that the exhibit had been kept overnight by the Wing On Company and that the writing on the label was in that of the Wing On Company.
Mr. Jenkin asked permission to call a witneas from the Wing On Company refuting this evidence and also that Professor Shell shear might be recalled to give evidence on this point.
His Lordship, however, held that this was not necessary.

label: text
text: PROPERTY CHANGES HANDS.

label: text
text: Further lots of the estate of the Jats Mr. M. J. D. Stephens (a solicitor who practised in Hongkong (for many years) have been sold by Measurad Deacons, the local legal firm.

label: text
text: A few weeks ago, it was reported in these columns that Stephens' Building together with several other lots on both sides of the harbour, had fetched $1,719,200, out of a total (anticipated) amount of over $5,000,000 for all of Mr. Stephens' property.

label: text
text: Since then, that big block of Chinese houses and shops opposite the present Central Fire Station, has been disposed of. There are over thirty houses in this block, with four frontages, along Des Vaux Road Central Pottinger Street, Queen's Road Central and Chinese Street.

label: text
text: At the time of the last report three of the houses in Connaught Road Central had remained unsold. These have also found new owners.

label: text
text: Together with other minor lots, and the previous amount, the total so far realised is about $8,250,000. Of this second lot, the big block of Chinese houses was the largest sale.

label: text
text: One case of small-pox and one of diphtheria (both Chinese) are reported during the 24 hours ended yesterday.

label: text
text: The Fire Brigade were called to an outbreak at the Italian Convent yesterday morning, occurring, it was reported, in a lift. Before the arrival of the Brigade, however, inmates had managed to extinguish the flames, and very little damage was done.

label: text
text: This concluding the case (at 1 o'clock) except for the final speeches and His Lordship's summing up, His Lordship asked Mr. C. G. Alabaster whether he would be the rest of the day with his speech.

label: text
text: Mr. Alabaster remarked that he was not sure but (with a smile) his theme "might run away with him."

label: text
text: Mr. Jenkin then raised one other point. If it was going to be the case, as one would gather from questions put to the second prisoner by Mr. Alabaster, that it was going to be contended that it would have been an impossibility for the books produced on behalf of the second prisoner to have been altered whilst the second prisoner was in jail he would have something to say about it.

label: text
text: His Lordship remarked that of course it was not an impossibility although the course would be attended with exceptional difficulty and he thought the matter best left to the common sense of the jury.

label: text
text: His Lordship then announced that instead of sitting throughout the day and all day to-morrow he thought it would be better to adjourn the case until Monday for the final speeches and summing

label: paragraph_title
text: Counsel's Objections.

label: text
text:
In the course of yesterday afternoon's cross-examination of Chan Kau, witness for the defence, Mr. Jenkin put it to witness that the paper inside the chopmark of one of the books relating to the accounts of the business of the second prisoner had been tampered with.
Mr. Alabaster, counsel for the defence, pointed out that similar questions had been put to three witnesses. If allegations were going to be made that something had been erased, the person should be named so that the defence could meet the case.
His Lordship said he understood it was suggested that a name had been erased but no particular person was named.
Mr. Jenkin said he would not dare to mention any one in particular without more time to go into the matter than he had had since the book came into his possession. He was merely asking the witnesses if they could see what he counsel, said he could see and asking for an explanation.
Continuing witness was closely crossed examined as to the manner in which the books of the firm were kept.
